finding.claim: Broken authorization: POST /admin/users/<uid>/ban runs do_ban for non-admin callers because the broad except swallows the 403 from require_admin.
finding.source: Any request to the ban route whose g.user is a dict with a falsy is_admin (any authenticated non-admin, or anonymous if auth sets a default dict). g.user is set outside this file.
finding.sink: do_ban(uid) at admin.py:20 (bans an arbitrary user)

trace.note: POST route registered with no auth decorator
abort(403) raises HTTPException when is_admin is falsy
except Exception catches the HTTPException (it subclasses Exception)
logs warning, does not re-raise or return

finding.guards_checked: require_admin raises correctly but its 403 is discarded by the broad except; no re-raise/early return; no decorator or before_request check in this file. unban (admin.py:24-28) has no try and propagates 403, so the two routes are inconsistent. Missing g.user yields AttributeError at admin.py:19 and a 500 before do_ban, so the bypass needs g.user to be a dict. Fix: call require_admin directly as unban does, or use a decorator.

verdict.guard_found: None effective. require_admin (admin.py:9-11) does raise abort(403) for a falsy is_admin, but it is called as a bare statement inside try (admin.py:16-17), and the broad except Exception (admin.py:18) catches the HTTPException and only logs (admin.py:19), so execution falls through to do_ban(uid) at admin.py:20. No decorator or before_request check exists in admin.py for the ban route (admin.py:14-15). The unban route (admin.py:24-26) calls require_admin without a try and is not affected, which shows the intended pattern.
verdict.reason: The trace matches the code: require_admin raises 403 at admin.py:11, the except Exception at admin.py:18-19 swallows it, and do_ban runs at admin.py:20 for any g.user whose is_admin is falsy, while unban at admin.py:26 correctly propagates the 403. The one caveat is that how g.user is populated lies outside this file, so whether an anonymous or ordinary authenticated caller reaches this path depends on code I could not read, but any non-admin dict-valued g.user reaches do_ban.

finding.claim: Sensitive data in logs: the failed admin check logs the caller's user name, which is PII, contrary to org policy.
finding.source: Any failed admin check on the ban route (same precondition as ADMIN-1).
finding.guards_checked: None. Fixing ADMIN-1 removes this path, but the log should use a user ID or drop the name.

verdict.guard_found: none. require_admin (admin.py:9-11) raises via abort(403), and the bare `except Exception` at admin.py:18 catches it, so the log.warning at admin.py:19 runs unconditionally. Nothing filters or redacts g.user.get("name") before it reaches the log.
verdict.reason: For any non-admin caller of the ban route, require_admin aborts at admin.py:11, the except at admin.py:18 swallows it, and admin.py:19 writes the caller's name to the log with no redaction, which is PII logging that the org policy prohibits; the severity is low because the only name written is the caller's own, and the attacker needs only a valid authenticated session, not admin rights.

finding.claim: Possible missing CSRF protection on state-changing POST routes (ban at line 14, unban at line 24), which could let a cross-site page ban users via an admin's browser session.
finding.source: Cross-origin form or fetch POST from an attacker page, using an admin's cookie-based session if one exists.
finding.sink: do_ban / do_unban at admin.py:20 and admin.py:27

trace.note: POST ban route accepts request with no token check in this file
POST unban route likewise has no token check

finding.guards_checked: Nothing in this file. Session mechanism and any app-wide CSRF or SameSite setting are not in the repo, so unverified.

verdict.guard_found: require_admin at admin.py:9-11 is the only check in the file. It raises via abort(403) on non-admins, but the ban route wraps it in try/except Exception at admin.py:16-19 and never returns, so do_ban at admin.py:20 runs anyway. The unban route at admin.py:26 has no try block, so its check is effective. No CSRF token check, SameSite setting, or session config exists in the repo.
verdict.reason: The line references are accurate, but the CSRF claim depends on session and CSRF config (for example Flask-WTF CSRFProtect or cookie SameSite) that is not in the repo, so it cannot be decided from this code. The file does show a stronger, verifiable bug the candidate missed: admin.py:16-19 swallows the abort(403) from require_admin (admin.py:11) so do_ban (admin.py:20) runs for any logged-in non-admin user, which is an authorization bypass rather than CSRF and does not need an admin victim.
